title: Assistant Secretary Chris Pilkerton's Remarks at ACI CFIUS Conference
summary: Assistant Secretary Chris Pilkerton outlined Treasury's priorities for CFIUS under the America First Investment Policy, emphasizing increased efficiency and reduced administrative burden for ally and partner transactions while maintaining rigorous national security review. The speech discussed the Known Investor Program for fast-track processing, enforcement of mandatory filing requirements, outreach on non-notified transactions, supply chain security collaboration, international cooperation on investment screening, and evolution of the Outbound Investment Security Program under the COINS Act.
key_points: CFIUS continues to balance national security protection with facilitating investment per the America's First Investment Policy
The Known Investor Program implements a 'fast track' process for transactions from verifiable allied investors
CFIUS is focused on enforcing mandatory filing requirements and identifying non-notified transactions that may raise national security concerns
The Outbound Investment Security Program will evolve per the COINS Act as passed with bipartisan support
Treasury plans to work with industry to inform vendor identification and capital deployment for secure domestic supply chains
CFIUS engagement with allies has led to establishment of dozens of investment screening mechanisms globally
why_it_matters: This speech signals specific enforcement priorities and program implementations under the current administration, including the operational rollout of the Known Investor Program and the COINS Act-driven evolution of outbound investment screening. CFIUS-related policy can affect cross-border M&A activity, capital flows, and sector-specific investment patterns (particularly in technology and critical infrastructure). While not a traditional macro catalyst, investment screening shifts are relevant to market participants in affected sectors.
macro_context: This speech discusses foreign investment policy rather than macro catalysts in the traditional finance sense. While investment screening can affect cross-border capital flows, this is primarily national security policy guidance with no immediate market-moving implications.
